items.prompt: Which measure counts the new cases of a disease that arise in a population at risk during a specified period?

options.label: Incidence
Odds ratio
Prevalence
Case-fatality rate

rubric: Incidence counts new cases over time in people at risk.
Prevalence counts existing cases, which is the usual confusion.

items.prompt: What term describes the proportion of a population that has a disease at a given point in time?

options.label: Prevalence
Incidence
Relative risk
Risk difference

rubric: Point prevalence is the share of people with the disease at one moment.
Incidence is often mixed up with it, but it counts only new cases.

items.prompt: Which study design starts by selecting people who have a disease and people who do not, then looks back at their past exposures?

options.label: Case-control study
Ecological study
Randomized controlled trial
Cohort study

rubric: Case-control studies sample by outcome and compare past exposure.
Cohort studies sample by exposure and follow people forward.

items.prompt: Which definition of a confounder is correct?

options.label: A variable recorded with error, so that cases are wrongly classified as non-cases in the study
A variable that arises only from random chance and fades as the sample of people grows larger
A variable caused by the exposure that lies on the pathway leading to the outcome
A variable linked to both exposure and outcome but not on the causal pathway

rubric: A confounder is associated with exposure and outcome and is not an intermediate step.
The last distractor describes a mediator, not a confounder.

items.prompt: Which is normally an early step in an outbreak investigation?

options.label: Publish the final findings in a peer-reviewed journal
Set up a permanent vaccination policy for the whole country
Confirm the diagnosis and verify that an outbreak exists
Randomly assign cases to different experimental treatments

rubric: Verifying the diagnosis and confirming an excess of cases comes early.
The other options are late steps or not part of an investigation.

items.prompt: Which of the following are measures of disease frequency? Select all that apply.

options.label: Incidence rate
Prevalence
Relative risk
Mortality rate
Odds ratio

rubric: Incidence, prevalence and mortality rates describe how often disease or death occurs.
Relative risk and odds ratio compare groups and are measures of association.

items.prompt: A health department surveys 1,000 residents on a single day and finds that 50 of them currently have diabetes. The department reports 5%. Which term names the measure it has reported?

options.label: Attack rate
Incidence rate
Prevalence
Case-fatality rate

rubric: A single-day survey of existing cases gives prevalence.
Incidence needs new cases followed over a period.

items.prompt: A cohort study reports a relative risk of 2.0 for a disease among exposed people. What does this mean?

options.label: Exactly two exposed people out of every three cases were caused by exposure
The exposed group has two more cases per 100 people than the unexposed
Two percent of exposed people go on to develop the disease in the study
The exposed group has twice the risk of the disease as the unexposed group

rubric: Relative risk is a ratio of risks in exposed and unexposed groups.
Confusing it with absolute risk or risk difference is the common error.

items.prompt: Why can a standard case-control study not directly estimate the incidence of disease?

options.label: Investigators choose the numbers of cases and controls, so the sample does not reflect population risk
Investigators include only people who have died, so the at-risk population is unknown to them
Investigators measure exposure with questionnaires, which always makes incidence impossible to compute
Investigators follow participants for too short a time to see enough new cases of disease

rubric: Sampling by outcome fixes the case-to-control ratio, so risk cannot be derived directly.
Case-control studies need not be short and do not rely only on deaths.

items.prompt: Researchers enroll 5,000 smokers and non-smokers free of lung cancer and follow them for 10 years, recording who develops it. How is this study best classified?

options.label: Case series
Case-control
Cross-sectional
Cohort study

rubric: Following exposed and unexposed groups forward in time is a cohort design.
Case-control studies begin with outcome status, not exposure.

items.prompt: A new treatment keeps patients with a chronic disease alive longer but does not cure them, and the incidence stays the same. What is the most likely effect on prevalence?

options.label: Prevalence rises only if the number of new cases also goes up
Prevalence rises because people stay in the diseased pool longer
Prevalence stays the same because incidence has not changed at all
Prevalence falls because fewer people are dying of the disease

rubric: Prevalence is roughly incidence times average duration, so longer survival raises it.
Assuming prevalence tracks incidence alone ignores duration.

items.prompt: In a case-control study of birth defects, mothers of affected babies remember and report past exposures more completely than mothers of healthy babies. Which type of bias is this?

options.label: Confounding, because a third variable is linked to both exposure and outcome
Selection bias, because controls were chosen differently from the cases
Information bias, because exposure was measured differently between groups
Random error, because a small sample size makes estimates imprecise

rubric: Differential recall of exposure between groups is recall bias.
Selection bias concerns who enters the study, not how well exposure is remembered.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe randomization in a clinical trial? Select all that apply.

options.label: It tends to balance both known and unknown confounders between groups
It makes participants unable to drop out of the trial
It guarantees that small trials have perfectly equal groups
It reduces the chance that group differences explain the outcome
It removes the need to measure outcomes accurately

rubric: Randomization balances confounders on average, including unmeasured ones.
It gives no guarantee in small trials and does not fix measurement or dropout.

items.prompt: After a wedding banquet, an investigator plots cases by onset time. The epidemic curve rises sharply to one peak and falls within a single incubation period. Which interpretation best fits this curve?

options.label: A point-source exposure, where many people were exposed at about the same time
A propagated outbreak, where person-to-person spread produces repeated waves of cases
An endemic pattern, where the disease occurs at a steady background level each year
A continuous exposure, where a contaminated source keeps infecting people for weeks

rubric: One sharp peak within one incubation period suggests a single common exposure.
Repeated waves point to person-to-person spread, and steady counts suggest endemic disease.

items.prompt: Which measure counts only new cases that arise during a defined period among people who were initially free of the disease?

options.label: Prevalence
Case fatality
Incidence
Proportional mortality

rubric: Incidence counts new cases in an at-risk population over time.
Prevalence counts existing cases, both old and new, which is the common confusion.

items.prompt: A new drug lets people with a chronic disease live much longer but does not cure it, and the number of new diagnoses per year stays the same. What happens to prevalence?

options.label: It falls first, because fewer patients die and are counted
It falls, because the drug reduces the burden of disease
It rises, because patients remain in the diseased state longer
It stays the same, because new diagnoses per year are unchanged

rubric: Prevalence is roughly incidence times average duration, so longer survival raises it.
Distractors confuse prevalence with incidence.

items.prompt: How does a case-control study differ in its starting point from a cohort study?

options.label: It starts by selecting people with the disease and comparing them with people without it
It starts by randomly assigning people to an exposure and measuring outcomes later
It starts by selecting exposed and unexposed people and following them for new disease
It starts by counting all cases and exposures in one whole population at one time

rubric: Case-control studies sample on outcome status and look back at exposure.
Cohort studies sample on exposure; the cross-sectional option is another common mix-up.

items.prompt: In a study of coffee drinking and lung cancer, smoking is linked to both coffee drinking and lung cancer. Why is smoking a confounder?

options.label: It is measured with error, which makes coffee intake look unrelated to cancer
It is more common in cases than in controls because of how they were chosen
It is associated with the exposure and the outcome and is not a step between them
It lies on the causal pathway from coffee drinking to the development of cancer

rubric: A confounder is linked to exposure and outcome and is not an intermediate on the causal path.
Measurement error, selection and mediators are different concepts.

items.prompt: In a case-control study of birth defects, mothers of affected babies recall medication use during pregnancy more completely than mothers of healthy babies. Which bias does this describe?

options.label: Recall bias
Lead-time bias
Healthy worker effect
Loss to follow-up

rubric: Differential recall of exposure between cases and controls is recall bias.
Other options are biases from different mechanisms.

items.prompt: Which of the following are features of a prospective cohort study? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is the most efficient design for studying very rare diseases
Risk ratios can be estimated directly from the results
Participants are followed over time to see who develops the outcome
Participants are selected because they already have the disease, then compared with people without it

items.prompt: During an outbreak of gastroenteritis after a wedding, the epidemic curve shows nearly all cases beginning within a span of about 10 hours, with one sharp peak. What does this pattern most suggest about the source?

options.label: Seasonal background illness unrelated to the wedding event
A point-source exposure, with most people exposed at about the same time
A propagated outbreak spreading person to person over several generations
A continuing common source with exposures spread over several weeks

rubric: A single sharp peak within one incubation range suggests one-time common exposure.
Person-to-person spread gives multiple successive peaks.

items.prompt: In a 5-year cohort study of a new respiratory illness, 30 of 200 exposed workers and 10 of 200 unexposed workers develop the disease. What is the risk ratio for exposed versus unexposed?
rubric: Risk exposed 0.15 divided by risk unexposed 0.05 equals 3.0.
2.0 is the risk difference in percentage points mistaken for a ratio; 0.33 inverts it.

items.prompt: In a case-control study, 40 of 100 cases and 20 of 100 controls were exposed. Using a 2x2 table, what is the odds ratio (to one decimal)?
rubric: 2.0 is the ratio of exposure proportions, which ignores the odds.

items.prompt: A survey on one day finds 50 people with asthma among 2,000 randomly sampled residents. What is the point prevalence?
rubric: Other values come from division or decimal errors.

items.prompt: A cohort records 12 new cases of diabetes over a total of 600 person-years of follow-up. What is the incidence rate?

options.label: 12 per 100 person-years
2 per 100 person-years
5 per 100 person-years
50 per 100 person-years

rubric: 12 / 600 = 0.02, which is 2 per 100 person-years.
Other options invert the fraction or misplace the scale.

items.prompt: An investigator has confirmed that a cluster of hepatitis A cases is an outbreak and verified the diagnoses. Which step comes next?

options.label: Test hypotheses with an analytic study
Implement control measures to stop the spread
Define a case and search for more cases
Communicate findings in a written report

rubric: After verifying the diagnosis, investigators write a case definition and find cases.
Hypothesis testing and reporting come later.

items.prompt: A study finds that coffee drinkers have more heart disease, and age is a suspected confounder. Which approaches control for age at the analysis stage? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adjust for age in a multivariable regression model
Randomly assign participants to drink coffee
Enlarge the sample after the data are collected
Stratify the results by age group

rubric: Stratification and regression adjustment are analysis-stage controls.
Randomization is a design-stage method, and a larger sample does not remove confounding.

items.prompt: After a picnic, 100 people were surveyed. Salad: 40 of 50 who ate it became ill, versus 5 of 50 who did not. Chicken: 30 of 60 who ate it became ill, versus 15 of 40 who did not. Which food is the most likely vehicle, based on attack rates?

options.label: Chicken, since its ill-to-well ratio is closest to even
Salad, since its attack rate is far higher in those who ate it
Neither, since some unexposed people also became ill
Chicken, since 30 ill people ate it, the most of any group

rubric: Salad: 80% vs 10% (RR 8); chicken: 50% vs 37.5% (RR 1.3), so salad fits best.
Absolute case counts and the presence of unexposed cases do not rule out a vehicle.

items.prompt: In a cohort study, 30 of 200 exposed people and 10 of 400 unexposed people developed the disease over five years. What is the risk ratio?
rubric: Risk in exposed is 30/200 = 0.15 and in unexposed 10/400 = 0.025, so RR = 6.0.
6.9 is the odds ratio, and 3.0 comes from comparing raw case counts.

items.prompt: In a case-control study, 40 of 60 cases and 10 of 50 controls were exposed. What is the odds ratio for exposure?
rubric: OR = (40 x 40)/(20 x 10) = 8.0 from exposed and unexposed cases and controls.
3.3 compares the proportions exposed, which is not the odds ratio.

items.prompt: A cohort of 500 people is followed and 20 develop the disease. Together they contribute 800 person-years at risk. What is the incidence rate?

options.label: 1.6 per 100 person-years
4.0 per 100 person-years
25 per 100 person-years
2.5 per 100 person-years

rubric: Rate = 20/800 = 2.5 per 100 person-years, using person-time as the denominator.
4.0 is the cumulative incidence (20/500), which ignores person-time.

items.prompt: In a stable population, a chronic disease has an incidence of 5 new cases per 1,000 people per year and an average duration of 4 years. What is the approximate prevalence?
rubric: Prevalence is approximately incidence x mean duration = 5 x 4 = 20 per 1,000.
Dividing by duration or repeating the incidence confuses the two measures.

items.prompt: A screening test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. It is used on 1,000 people in whom disease prevalence is 10%. What proportion of positive results are true positives?
rubric: There are 90 true positives and 45 false positives, so PPV = 90/135, about 67%.
90% is the sensitivity, which ignores the base rate and false positives.

items.prompt: Investigators fix their sample at 100 cases and 200 controls and record exposure in each. Which quantities can they validly calculate from these data? Select all that apply.

options.label: The proportion of controls who were exposed
The risk ratio computed directly from the 2x2 counts
The incidence of disease among exposed people
The odds ratio of exposure for cases compared with controls

rubric: Case-control sampling allows the odds ratio and the exposure prevalence among controls.
Incidence and direct risk ratios need the population at risk, which this sampling does not provide.

items.prompt: After a banquet of 100 guests, 42 developed gastroenteritis. Of 40 who ate salad, 30 were ill, versus 12 of 60 who did not. Of 80 who ate chicken, 38 were ill, versus 4 of 20 who did not. Which food is the more likely vehicle?

options.label: Salad: its attack-rate ratio of 3.8 exceeds chicken's 2.4
Chicken: 38 of the 42 ill guests ate it, more than ate salad
Neither: both foods show a ratio above 1, so the data cannot separate them
Chicken: it was eaten by more guests, so it had more chances to spread illness

rubric: Compare attack rates in eaters and non-eaters: salad 75% vs 20% (3.8), chicken 47.5% vs 20% (2.4).
Counting ill eaters ignores how many people ate each food.

items.prompt: An observational study finds that adults who take daily vitamin supplements have 30% lower heart disease rates. Supplement users also exercise more and smoke less. Which explanation best fits?

options.label: Effect modification: supplements work differently in exercisers than non-exercisers
Confounding: lifestyle is linked to both supplement use and heart disease
Selection bias: supplement users were more likely to be lost to follow-up
Recall bias: users remember their heart symptoms more accurately than non-users

rubric: Exercise and smoking are associated with both exposure and outcome, which is confounding.
Effect modification would need the supplement effect to differ across strata, which is not described.

items.prompt: A cohort of factory workers has lower all-cause mortality than the general population, although the factory uses a known carcinogen. What best explains the low mortality?

options.label: The carcinogen protects against other causes of death, lowering overall mortality
The general population has higher mortality because it contains many more smokers than the workforce
Loss to follow-up among the healthiest workers removed their survivors from the cohort count
Only healthy people get hired, so the general population is not a like-for-like comparison

rubric: This is the healthy worker effect: employment selects healthier people, so the general population is a poor comparison group.
The other options invent mechanisms not supported by the scenario.

items.prompt: A study reports a crude risk ratio of 2.5 for an exposure and a disease. Stratified by sex, the risk ratio is 4.0 in men and 1.2 in women. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Sex modifies the effect, so stratum-specific estimates should be reported, not one summary
The crude estimate is correct because it lies between the two stratum-specific values
Sex confounds the association, so one sex-adjusted summary estimate should be reported
The strata differ only through chance, so the crude ratio should be reported without comment

rubric: Markedly different stratum-specific ratios indicate effect modification, which a single summary would hide.
Confounding is handled by adjustment, but adjusting here would mask a real difference.

items.prompt: A screening programme raises five-year survival after diagnosis from 60% to 80%, yet population mortality from the disease is unchanged. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Confounding: screened people are older and so survive longer after diagnosis
Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens survival time without delaying death
Length bias: screening finds only fast-growing tumours that kill sooner
Recall bias: screened patients report their survival more favourably than others

rubric: Earlier detection starts the survival clock sooner, so survival rises while death occurs at the same time.
Length bias would favour slow-growing tumours, not fast-growing ones.

items.prompt: A hospital-based case-control study picks controls from patients admitted for other conditions. Many of those conditions are also caused by the exposure under study. What is the likely effect on the result?

options.label: Cases are under-ascertained because milder cases are never admitted, so the odds ratio is biased away from the null
Controls are over-exposed relative to the population, so the odds ratio is biased toward the null
Interviewers probe cases harder than controls about past exposure, so the odds ratio is biased away from the null
Confounding by age arises, so the odds ratio is biased in an unpredictable direction

rubric: This is Berkson-type selection bias: controls share the exposure, which inflates their exposure and shrinks the odds ratio.
The other options name biases that this selection mechanism does not create.

items.prompt: An investigator examines an epidemic curve. Which findings point to a point-source outbreak rather than a propagated one? Select all that apply.

options.label: Successive waves of cases spaced about one incubation period apart
Case numbers stay level for several years at a stable rate
Most cases attended the same event on one day
Cases rise and fall within roughly one incubation period

rubric: A single sharp peak within one incubation period and a shared exposure indicate a common point source.
Repeated waves suggest person-to-person spread, and a level rate over years suggests endemic disease.

items.prompt: A five-year cohort compares lung function decline in 500 exposed and 500 unexposed workers. Thirty percent of exposed workers left the study, mostly because they became too ill to attend visits. The analysis finds only a small difference between groups. What is the most likely problem?

options.label: Recall bias, because exposed workers over-report their symptoms at each follow-up visit and exaggerate the decline
Lead-time bias, because earlier detection of decline lengthens the apparent follow-up time in the exposed group
Confounding by age, because older workers are more likely to be exposed and also decline faster in lung function
Informative loss to follow-up removed the sickest exposed workers, biasing toward the null

rubric: Dropout related to both exposure and outcome removes the worst-affected exposed workers, shrinking the observed effect.
Lung function is measured, so recall bias does not apply, and confounding does not always inflate effects.

items.prompt: A case-control study of coffee intake and pancreatic cancer recruits controls from patients on a gastroenterology ward. Many of them have ulcers or reflux and avoid coffee. Which problem best explains why the odds ratio may be inflated?

options.label: Cases recall past coffee use more accurately than controls, so differential recall bias
Controls do not represent the exposure distribution of the source population, so selection bias
Pancreatic cancer is rare, so the odds ratio cannot approximate a relative risk
Age differs between cases and controls, so residual confounding by age occurs

rubric: Controls with GI disease under-represent coffee drinking, which is a control selection bias that inflates the OR.
Recall bias and the rare-disease assumption are distinct issues not raised by the setup.

items.prompt: In a 10-year cohort, exposed participants who develop early symptoms of the outcome are more likely to drop out and are not followed up. Unexposed participants drop out at random. What is the likely effect on the observed risk ratio?

options.label: Underestimate, because exposed cases are missing from the exposed numerator
Overestimate, because person-time is lost mostly from the unexposed group
No change, because loss to follow-up affects both groups' denominators equally
Overestimate, because the exposed group keeps only its healthiest members

rubric: Differential loss of exposed cases removes events from the exposed group, biasing the RR toward the null.
Distractors assume loss is non-informative or reverse the direction.

items.prompt: A crude analysis shows a risk ratio of 1.8 for heavy drinking and lung cancer. Within each smoking stratum (smokers, non-smokers) the risk ratio is 1.0. Drinkers smoke more often. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Selection bias, since smokers are over-represented among drinkers
Mediation by smoking, since drinking leads to smoking, which causes cancer
Confounding by smoking, since it is linked to drinking and causes lung cancer
Effect modification by smoking, since the stratum RRs differ from the crude RR

rubric: The crude association vanishes within strata, and smoking relates to both exposure and outcome, which is confounding.
Effect modification requires stratum RRs that differ from each other, not merely from the crude RR.

items.prompt: A drug's risk ratio for an adverse event is 3.0 in men and 0.8 in women. The crude RR is 1.5. The sex distribution is the same in treated and untreated groups. What is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.label: Sex is a mediator on the causal path, so adjust for it to isolate the drug's direct effect on the event
Sex is a confounder of the drug-event link, so report only the sex-adjusted pooled estimate as the result
Sex is an effect modifier, so report stratum-specific estimates rather than one pooled figure
The study has selection bias by sex, so the strata should be discarded as unreliable and the crude RR used

rubric: Very different stratum RRs with balanced sex indicate effect modification, so stratum-specific estimates are informative.
A single pooled adjusted figure would hide the opposite effects.

items.prompt: After a wedding banquet, an epidemic curve of gastroenteritis shows one sharp peak with nearly all cases falling within a span shorter than the disease's incubation range. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?

options.label: A continuous common-source exposure lasting several weeks
A point-source exposure, with most people exposed at about the same time
A propagated outbreak through person-to-person spread over several generations
An endemic baseline fluctuation unrelated to a particular event

rubric: A single steep peak within one incubation range indicates simultaneous exposure to a common source.
Propagated spread produces successive waves spaced by the incubation period.

items.prompt: An observational study compares outcomes between two treatments and wants to control for a measured confounder at the analysis stage. Which approaches are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.label: Adjusting for an intermediate variable on the causal path from treatment to outcome
Multivariable regression including the confounder as a covariate
Random allocation of participants to treatment groups
Mantel-Haenszel stratification by levels of the confounder

rubric: Stratification and regression are analysis-stage confounder controls.
Adjusting for a mediator blocks part of the true effect, and randomization is a design-stage method, not analysis.

items.prompt: A cancer screening programme reports that five-year survival after diagnosis rose from 55% to 80% among screened people. Population cancer mortality rates over the same period did not change. Screening detects tumours earlier but no new treatment was introduced. Which explanation best accounts for these findings?

options.label: Lead-time bias, because earlier diagnosis lengthens measured survival without delaying death
Information bias, because cause of death is misclassified on death certificates of screened people
Recall bias, because screened people remember the timing of their symptom onset more accurately
Confounding by age, because screened people are older at diagnosis and so survive for longer

rubric: Survival is counted from diagnosis, so earlier detection inflates survival even when death time is unchanged; unchanged mortality supports this.
The other biases do not explain the divergence between survival and mortality.

items.prompt: Researchers want to study many possible risk factors for a disease with an incidence of 2 per 100,000 per year. Budget is limited and rapid results are needed. Judged against these criteria, which design is best?

options.label: A prospective cohort, because exposures are measured before disease occurs and recall bias is avoided
A cross-sectional survey, because it estimates incidence directly and is quick and cheap to run
A case-control study, because it is efficient for rare outcomes and can assess many exposures
A randomised trial, because random allocation removes confounding for every exposure studied

rubric: For rare outcomes with limited budget and time, case-control sampling by outcome is efficient and allows multiple exposures.
A cohort would need huge numbers, and cross-sectional surveys measure prevalence, not incidence.

items.prompt: A paper compares 20 countries and finds that national average fat intake correlates strongly with breast cancer rates. The authors conclude that eating more fat raises an individual woman's risk. Which critique is most decisive?

options.label: Fat intake should have been measured as a binary exposure, because continuous averages cannot be linked to incidence rates
Country-level correlation does not show the same link in individuals
Correlation coefficients are invalid between rates and averages, because the two variables are measured on different scales
With only 20 countries the sample is too small, so no correlation could be reliably computed or interpreted

rubric: Ecological data cannot establish individual-level links because group averages hide who ate the fat and who got the disease.
Sample size and variable coding are minor compared with the inferential leap.

items.prompt: A new drug cuts the risk of an event from 2% to 1% over five years. A health agency must decide whether to fund it for a large low-risk population, given a high drug cost. Which summary best serves that decision?

options.label: The p-value for the difference, since a very small p-value shows the benefit is large enough to justify the cost
The relative risk reduction of 50%, since it stays the same whatever the baseline risk and so transfers to any population
The absolute risk reduction of 1 point (NNT 100), since benefit per treated person depends on baseline risk
The odds ratio of about 0.5, since odds are more stable across populations and so predict benefit anywhere

rubric: Absolute risk reduction and NNT reflect real benefit per person treated and cost, especially in low-risk groups.
RRR can sound large when baseline risk is small, and p-values do not measure effect size.

items.prompt: A test for a disease with 0.1% prevalence has 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity. A programme proposes testing everyone and treating all positives with an invasive procedure. Which judgement is best supported?

options.label: Acceptable, since specificity above 90% guarantees that most positive results are true cases
Problematic, since PPV is only about 2%, so most positives are false
Acceptable, since 95% accuracy means that most people who test positive truly have the disease
Unacceptable, since sensitivity of 95% is too low to detect most true cases in a population

rubric: PPV is roughly 0.00095/0.0509, about 1.9%, so false positives dominate at low prevalence.
Distractors confuse sensitivity or specificity with predictive value.

items.prompt: During a salmonella outbreak, interviews show that 80% of ill people ate a particular brand of sprouts versus 10% of well people. Illness is severe and the product is still on shelves. Lab confirmation will take days. What is the best immediate action?

options.label: Survey a random sample of all consumers first, so that the intervention rests on unbiased population estimates
Wait for lab confirmation of the source, since acting on interview data alone risks recall of the wrong product
Warn the public and pull the product now, while continuing to collect confirmatory evidence
Restrict only hospital food supplies, since severe cases are the ones that get hospitalised and reported

rubric: A strong exposure association, ongoing risk and severity justify acting on the available evidence while confirming.
Waiting for lab results delays prevention of further cases.

items.prompt: In a randomised trial, 30% of participants dropped out, more in the treatment arm because of side effects. The authors report only a per-protocol analysis showing large benefit. Which critiques are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: Analysis by intention to treat would better preserve randomisation for estimating effectiveness
Per-protocol analysis is always preferable because it measures only true drug effect
Participants who tolerate the drug may differ systematically, so benefit is likely overstated
Excluding non-completers breaks the balance created by randomisation, so the groups are no longer comparable

rubric: Per-protocol analysis with differential dropout introduces selection bias, and intention-to-treat preserves the randomised comparison.
The claim that per-protocol is always preferable ignores this bias.

items.prompt: A cohort study finds that statin users have 40% lower dementia incidence than non-users after adjusting for age, sex and smoking. Critics suggest that people with early undiagnosed cognitive decline are less likely to be prescribed or to adhere to statins. Which analysis best tests this criticism?

options.label: Enlarge the cohort several-fold so the confidence interval around the 40% reduction becomes much narrower
Repeat the analysis excluding the first several years of follow-up, so early dementia cannot influence statin use
Add further covariates such as education, income and physical activity to the model to adjust for more confounders
Compare dementia incidence among non-users across regions to check whether background risk varies geographically

rubric: A lag-time analysis checks for reverse causation by removing outcomes that might have preceded statin use.
More precision or further adjustment cannot fix reverse causation.

items.prompt: A case-control study of occupational solvent exposure and bladder cancer must choose controls. Criterion: the odds ratio should estimate the exposure–disease relation in the population that produced the cases. Which control strategy best meets this criterion?

options.label: Friends nominated by the cases, to match on social background and lifestyle
Patients admitted to the same hospital for solvent-related skin conditions
Random sample of residents from the catchment area that generated the cases
Cases' co-workers, since they share the workplace and so improve comparability

rubric: Controls should represent the exposure distribution of the source population that gave rise to the cases.
Hospital controls with exposure-related illness and co-workers distort exposure prevalence and bias the odds ratio.

items.prompt: A cohort study finds that regular exercise lowers cardiovascular mortality. Analysts also adjust for blood pressure, which exercise lowers and which causes cardiovascular death, and report the result as the total effect of exercise. Which critique is most valid?

options.label: Blood pressure should be adjusted for because a variable associated with both exposure and outcome is a confounder
Adjusting for a mediator blocks part of the effect, so the estimate is biased toward the null
Adjusting for blood pressure mainly improves precision, so the total effect estimate is not materially changed
Adjustment is valid because blood pressure was measured before the outcome occurred in these subjects

rubric: Blood pressure lies on the causal path, so adjusting removes the mediated portion and estimates only a direct effect.
Distractors treat any associated variable as a confounder, ignoring causal structure.

items.prompt: Among hospitalised patients, researchers find diabetes and a certain fracture type are inversely associated. Neither condition alone is unusual in the community. Which judgement best explains the finding as a likely artefact?

options.label: Diabetes protects bone, as the association is strong and statistically significant across the hospital sample
Confounding by age explains it, since older patients are admitted more often and have more of both conditions
Either condition can cause admission, so restricting to inpatients induces Berkson's selection bias
Fracture patients are misclassified as non-diabetic because hospital record keeping is poor for diabetes status

rubric: Conditioning on hospital admission, a common effect of both conditions, creates a spurious association between them.
Age confounding or misclassification would not specifically arise from restricting to a common effect.

items.prompt: A screening programme reports that five-year survival after diagnosis rose from 60% to 85% in screened cohorts. Criterion: the evidence must show screening actually reduces deaths from the disease. Which evidence best meets it?

options.label: Greater number of cases found per 1000 screened, showing the test reaches hidden disease
Higher proportion of early-stage tumours detected at diagnosis in screened people overall
Longer survival from diagnosis among screen-detected cases than among clinically detected cases
Lower disease-specific mortality in a randomised trial of invited versus not-invited people

rubric: Mortality in a randomised comparison is immune to lead-time and length-time bias and overdiagnosis.
Survival, stage shift and detection counts can all rise without any reduction in deaths.

items.prompt: A rapid test has 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity. A colleague says that in any setting 95% of positive results are true cases, and plans to use it to screen a population where prevalence is 0.5%. Which judgement is correct?

options.label: The claim holds; with both at 95%, about 95% of positives are true cases in any population screened
The claim holds once the sample is large enough to remove random error, giving PPV near 95%
The claim fails mainly because screening needs sensitivity above specificity, which would raise PPV to 95%
The claim fails; PPV depends on prevalence and would be under 10% at 0.5% prevalence

rubric: At 0.5% prevalence, true positives ≈0.475 per 100 versus ≈4.975 false positives, giving PPV near 9%.
The distractors confuse sensitivity/specificity with predictive values or blame sample size.

items.prompt: A cohort study compares influenza hospitalisation between vaccinated and unvaccinated older adults using health records and finds a large protective effect. Which critiques of a causal reading are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: A large effect estimate proves the absence of confounding, since bias is small relative to it
Using a risk ratio rather than an odds ratio invalidates any such comparison
Differential care seeking may alter how often outcomes are recorded in each group
Unmeasured frailty confounding may remain even after adjusting for age and sex
Healthy-vaccinee bias: frailer people may be less likely to be vaccinated

rubric: Healthy-vaccinee bias, differential ascertainment and residual frailty confounding are recognised threats in observational vaccine studies.
Effect measure choice does not invalidate a comparison, and large effects do not rule out bias.

items.prompt: After a banquet of 60 guests, 24 became ill. Of 30 who ate the potato salad, 22 were ill; of 30 who did not, 2 were ill. Of 50 who ate the chicken, 23 were ill; of 10 who did not, 1 was ill. Which judgement about the likely vehicle is best supported?

options.label: Both equally, since each has a higher attack rate in exposed than unexposed guests
Neither, since with only 60 guests chance could explain any difference in rates
Potato salad, since its risk ratio is about 11 and few unexposed guests fell ill
Chicken, since 23 of the 24 ill guests ate it, so it explains nearly all cases

rubric: Salad attack rate 73% vs 7% (RR about 11) versus chicken 46% vs 10% (RR about 4.6); most chicken eaters also ate salad.
Chicken has the most ill eaters only because nearly everyone ate it.

items.prompt: A large cohort has stored baseline serum. Constraints: the outcome (pancreatic cancer) is rare, the biomarker assay is costly, and the study must keep temporal order and control for person-time. Which design best fits?

options.label: Case-control study using living cases from clinics and community volunteers as controls, assaying fresh blood from all of them
Nested case-control study with incidence-density sampling of controls, assaying only cases and matched controls
Full cohort analysis assaying stored serum from every participant, so that no person-time or exposure data is lost
Cross-sectional survey of current participants, comparing biomarker levels by disease status at a single time point

rubric: Nested case-control within the cohort preserves temporal order and source population while assaying a small subset.
The other designs are costly, lose temporality, or sample controls from a different base.

items.prompt: You must estimate the effect of a treatment on survival where disease severity changes over time, affects later treatment decisions, and is itself affected by earlier treatment. Which analysis plan meets this constraint?

options.label: Propensity-score matching on baseline characteristics only, to mimic a randomised trial at time zero
Marginal structural model with inverse-probability-of-treatment weights from time-varying covariates
Stratify on severity at each visit and pool the stratum-specific hazard ratios with Mantel-Haenszel weights
Cox model with baseline covariates plus current severity entered as an ordinary time-varying covariate

rubric: Time-varying confounding affected by prior treatment needs g-methods such as marginal structural models.
Conventional adjustment or stratification on severity blocks mediated effects and introduces bias.

items.prompt: A cluster of severe illness appears with an unknown pathogen. Constraints: investigators need to find cases early, must not miss them, but also need a basis for later analytic comparisons. Which case-definition plan best meets these?

options.label: A definition based on exposure to the suspected venue alone, to avoid circular reasoning
A broad symptom-based definition kept fixed throughout, so that counts and rates stay comparable across the whole outbreak
A tiered definition of suspected, probable and confirmed cases, starting broad and tightening as data accrue
A single narrow definition requiring a lab-confirmed test, to keep every counted case certain

rubric: Tiered definitions preserve sensitivity early and specificity later while allowing sensitivity analyses.
A narrow lab-only or fixed definition misses cases or dilutes later analyses; exposure-based definitions are circular.

items.prompt: Design requirement: measure both the direct protection of a new vaccine and its indirect (herd) effect in villages with frequent contact between households. Which trial design satisfies it?

options.label: Individually randomised placebo trial within each village, comparing vaccinated and placebo individuals only
Open-label rollout to volunteers, compared with non-volunteers in the same village
Cluster-randomised trial by village, with outcomes measured among both vaccinated and unvaccinated residents
Before-after comparison in a single village, which removes between-village differences

rubric: Randomising whole villages allows comparison of unvaccinated residents across arms, capturing indirect effects.
Individual randomisation within villages cannot separate indirect effects because arms mix.

items.prompt: A proposed study compares cancer rates in people currently taking a drug with people not taking it, using existing prescription records for prevalent users. Which design change would best reduce bias from survivors and indication?

options.label: Restricting to participants aged 65 or younger, which removes most confounding by age
A new-user design with an active comparator, starting follow-up at treatment initiation
A larger sample, since power is the main limit on validity in prevalent-user comparisons
Adjustment for the number of prescriptions filled, as a measure of duration of exposure

rubric: New-user, active-comparator designs align time zero and reduce depletion of susceptibles and confounding by indication.
Sample size, age exclusion and adjusting for duration do not fix these structural biases.

items.prompt: A cohort study classifies patients as exposed if they filled a drug prescription at any time within one year after diagnosis, and follows everyone from diagnosis. Exposed people appear to survive longer. Which redesigns address the resulting immortal-time bias? Select all that apply.

options.label: Classify exposure as time-varying, so person-time before the first fill counts as unexposed
Start follow-up at diagnosis for the unexposed but at first fill for the exposed
Emulate a target trial by aligning time zero with treatment assignment for both groups
Exclude all deaths in the first year to equalise the follow-up in the two groups
Use a landmark analysis, classifying exposure at a fixed time and following only those alive then

rubric: Time-varying exposure, landmark analysis and target-trial alignment all remove the guaranteed-survival period from exposed person-time.
Different start points or excluding early deaths create new bias rather than solving it.

items.prompt: During a respiratory epidemic, a health agency wants a rapid estimate of a new vaccine's effectiveness. Randomisation is impossible, vaccination status is in registry data, and people who seek testing differ from the general population in care-seeking behaviour. Which design best meets these constraints?

options.label: Survey vaccinated people about symptoms after vaccination and compare their attack rate with historical attack rates from earlier seasons
Test-negative design among symptomatic tested people, comparing vaccination in test-positives and test-negatives, adjusted for calendar time
Cohort comparison of infection rates in vaccinated and unvaccinated registry residents, adjusted for age and sex but using all recorded test results
Compare vaccine coverage among all confirmed cases with national coverage figures, standardised by age group to remove confounding

rubric: Restricting to symptomatic people who sought testing balances care-seeking, and adjustment for calendar time handles changing incidence.
Comparisons with national coverage, unadjusted registry rates or historical rates ignore testing and care-seeking differences.
